say: Growth, people and proof.
This is the video for module 3 of Production Scaling and Quality Assurance.
A school asks for 400 packs by Friday. A supermarket asks for 300 packs every Monday, for months. Breaking that promise once can lose the account.

say: Plan with demonstrated capacity: what you actually produced to specification in a normal week. For Kemi, 2,100 packs a week.

panel.heading: Should Kemi take 500 more packs a week?

say: Utilisation is committed demand divided by capacity. She already supplies 1,500 packs, so 71%.

panel.heading: Should Kemi take 500 more packs a week?

say: A supermarket wants 500 more every Monday. That is 95%, with only 100 packs spare.

panel.heading: Should Kemi take 500 more packs a week?

say: Her records show she loses about one day a month to power cuts and illness. One lost day is 420 packs. With 100 spare, recovery takes more than 4 weeks.

panel.heading: Should Kemi take 500 more packs a week?

say: So she offers 300 a week for 6 weeks. That leaves 300 spare, and a lost day is recovered in 1.4 weeks. After 6 weeks of on-time delivery, she has evidence for more.

panel.heading: Should Kemi take 500 more packs a week?
panel.rule: Let the volume follow your evidence, never run ahead of it.

say: Keep a small buffer of passed product so a bad day does not become a missed delivery. Label every carton, and always deliver the oldest good stock first.

say: For a one-off order, divide it by your spare capacity, then add buying and delivery time. Kemi quotes 4 weeks plus delivery, not 1 week.
And watch long payment terms: waiting 30 days means you fund the stock yourself.

say: Some food faults can never be reworked. Anything dropped, contaminated, mouldy or past its date is scrapped.
Never hide a food safety problem. Find the cause, and if it was sold, contact the buyers.

say: Keep a defect log. Over two weeks Kemi's team logs 100 defective packs out of about 4,000.
Sort them largest first. Burnt and broken packs cause 76% of all defects. This is a Pareto table. It shows where to spend your effort.
Then a 20-minute fishbone session: the team lists possible causes under people, equipment, method, materials, measurement and environment.
The defect log shows most burnt packs came from the last loads of the day, when the fryer was tired and the oil oldest.
Her corrective actions: a fryer rotation every two hours, oil changed at a fixed number of loads, and the timer reset written into the method. Two weeks later, she checks the log again.

panel.heading: Pareto, then fishbone
panel.rule: A correction fixes the product. A corrective action removes the cause.

say: To remember. Promise from demonstrated capacity, with a cushion and a buffer. Hold failed items and follow rework rules. Remove causes with Pareto and fishbone. And put a lot code on every pack.
